content.text:
Here's the full technical picture, in layers. Learn these five and you can field anything.

---

## Layer 1 — What `entire-graph` builds (you depend on this, don't reimplement it)

`entire-graph` parses every file with **tree-sitter** (real grammars, not regex) and emits a **typed graph**:

- **Nodes** = symbols: functions, methods, classes, types, fields — each with a stable id, `qualified_name`, `file:line`, language, kind.
- **Edges** = ~30 relation types. The ones you use:
  | edge | meaning |
  |---|---|
  | `CALLS` | A calls B (resolved from the call site, tree-sitter-accurate) |
  | `USES_TYPE` / `PARAM_TYPE` / `RETURNS_TYPE` | A references type B in its body / params / return |
  | `DATA_FLOWS` | a value flows from A to B (param forwarding, return threading) |
  | `FILE_CHANGES_WITH` | A's file and B's file historically change in the same commits (mined from git log) |
  | `CONTAINS` | class A contains method B (→ "siblings") |

It's **deterministic and local** — same repo + same commit = same graph, no model, no network. That matters for a judge: "our impact analysis isn't an LLM guessing, it's a parsed call graph."

---

## Layer 2 — What you ask it, per changed symbol

Two commands:

**`entire-graph diff --base <A> --head <B> --json`** → the list of changed symbols. Each row:
```json
{ "name": "Database.query", "kind": "method", "type": "signature_changed",
  "after_start_line": 12, "dependents_count": 6 }
```
`dependents_count` is entire-graph's own heuristic count of things that transitively depend on this symbol.

**`entire-graph impact --symbol "Database.query" --file src/db/database.ts --depth 2 --format json`** → a **bounded traversal outward from that one symbol**, already sectioned:
```
callers        (who calls it — incoming CALLS, depth ≤ 2)
callees        (what it calls — outgoing CALLS)
type_consumers (USES_TYPE / PARAM_TYPE / RETURNS_TYPE)
data_flows     (DATA_FLOWS edges)
co_changes     (FILE_CHANGES_WITH — git co-change)
siblings       (same CONTAINS parent)
```

Real output for `Database.query` in the demo:
```
callers (5):  LinkRepo.byId (depth 1), LinkRepo.save (1), LinkRepo.hit (1),
              RedirectService.resolve (2, via LinkRepo.byId),
              ShortenService.create (2, via LinkRepo.save)
type_consumers (4): Row (RETURNS_TYPE), QueryOptions (PARAM_TYPE), ...
co_changes (3):  <3 files that change alongside src/db/database.ts>
siblings (1):    Database.seed
```

So **`entire-graph` does the graph walk**. You don't traverse edges yourself — you call `impact` once per changed symbol.

---

## Layer 3 — Your code: turning one impact result into radius nodes

`src/domain/graph-mapping.ts` → `toRadiusNodes(rawImpact, "Database.query")`:

For every entry in every section, it produces a `RadiusNode`:
```ts
{
  ref: { qualifiedName: "LinkRepo.byId", file: "src/repo/link-repo.ts", line: 8, ... },
  section: "callers",
  relation: "CALLED_BY",           // section → relation mapping
  direction: "in",
  distance: 1,                      // = entire-graph's depth (1 = direct)
  viaChain: ["LinkRepo.byId"],      // intermediate hops, from the `via` field
  callSite: { file: "...", line: 14 },
  originSymbols: ["Database.query"], // ← tagged with WHICH changed symbol this came from
  isTest: false                     // matched against test-file globs
}
```

Key move: **every node is stamped with its origin** (`originSymbols`). That's what lets you later say "this test covers `Database.query` and `LinkRepo.byId`."

---

## Layer 4 — The fold: `computeBlastRadius()` (`src/domain/blast-radius.ts`)

You call `impact` for *each* changed symbol, so you get N node-lists that **overlap**. This function merges them into one deduplicated set. The exact algorithm:

```
byKey = {}                          // Map<"file::qualifiedName", RadiusNode>
originKeys  = {every changed symbol's key}
originNames = {every changed symbol's qualified name}
addedNames  = {changed symbols whose type == "added"}

for each node in every list:
    1. DROP if node is an external callee        (fmt.Errorf etc. — noise)
    2. DROP if node is a sibling of an added-only symbol   (members of a new class)
    3. DROP if node IS one of the changed symbols          (it's the origin, not the blast)
    4. key = "<file>::<qualifiedName>"
       if key already seen → mergeNode(existing, incoming):
           - keep the SHORTER distance
           - UNION the originSymbols
           - keep whichever has a real viaChain / callSite
           - isTest = either was a test
       else → store it

nodes = values(byKey) sorted by (distance asc, then name)
sectionTotals[section] = count of nodes in that section
```

So the **19 nodes** in your report = distinct `(file, symbol)` pairs across all 4 impact calls (Database.query, LinkRepo.byId, .save, .hit — wait, 4 changed callables + the added ones), after dropping origins/externals/added-siblings and merging duplicates.

Why dedup by `(file, qualifiedName)` and not just name: two different `query` methods in different files are different nodes; the same `LinkRepo.byId` reached from both `Database.query` and (transitively) another change is **one** node with `originSymbols: ["Database.query", ...]` and the shortest distance kept.

---

## Layer 5 — What the numbers in the report mean

| Report says | Computed from |
|---|---|
| **19 nodes** | `radius.nodes.length` |
| **8 modules** | distinct first-2 path segments across those nodes (`summary.ts`) |
| **CALLED_BY: 8 · RETURNS_TYPE: 3 · …** | `groupBy(node.relation)` |
| **`Database.query` … 6 dependents** | `dependents_count` straight from `entire-graph diff` |
| **evidence path `Database.query → ShortenService.create`** | `[originSymbol, ...node.viaChain, node.name]` for the nearest caller nodes |
| **`link-repo.test.ts` covers Database.query, LinkRepo.byId, …** | that test node's `originSymbols` (accumulated during the merge) |

---

## Be honest about the limits (judges respect this)

1. **Call resolution is static.** Dynamic dispatch, reflection, DI containers, string-keyed handlers → edges can be missed or over-approximated. entire-graph is tree-sitter-accurate for direct calls; it degrades gracefully and reports `completeness: degraded` in its JSON.
2. **`depth 2` cap.** You see direct + one hop of transitive callers, not the whole tree. Deliberate — deeper is noise for a review.
3. **`co_changes` are heuristic** (git history correlation), not causal.
4. **`dependents_count`** is entire-graph's number, not independently verified by you — you surface it, you don't recompute it.
5. **"covers every changed symbol"** means *a test exists that transitively reaches it in the graph* — not that the test asserts on the new behavior. It's test *selection*, not coverage measurement.

If a judge pushes on accuracy: *"It's a static call graph, so it's precise for direct calls and conservative elsewhere — the same tradeoff every IDE 'find usages' makes. We surface the graph path for every claim so the reviewer verifies, rather than trusting."*
Any scope to make it better?

Yes — plenty. Here's the map, ordered by effort-vs-payoff. The first group is doable before submission today.

## Quick wins (each < 1 hr, real demo impact)

| Improvement | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Dedupe the evidence lines** | Right now when two strategies fire on one symbol you see near-duplicate "reaches X" / "dependents include X". Merge them. Pure polish, but the evidence block is what a judge reads closely. |
| **Show the call sites to fix** | `entire-graph` already gives `call_site: {file, line}` for every caller. For a `signature_changed` symbol, emit a checklist: *"9 call sites to update: `link-repo.ts:14`, `link-repo.ts:24`, …"*. Turns the tool from "warning" into "actionable." |
| **Name the `co_changes` files** | Those `FILE_CHANGES_WITH` entries currently have blank names (they're file edges, not symbols). Render them as `↔ src/http/router.ts` instead of dropping the label. |
| **"Review in this order" list** | Add one ordered checklist at the top: highest-severity finding → widest change → coverage gaps. Reviewers want a path, not a table. |
| **Breaking-change flag** | Compare old vs new signature: param added without default, return type narrowed, param removed → tag the finding `breaking`. `diff` already gives `old_signature`/`new_signature`. |

## Real improvements (0.5–2 days each — future-work slide)

1. **Smarter scope-creep than lexical overlap.**
   - **Graph-anchored:** if a changed symbol is 1–2 hops in the call graph from a symbol that *does* match the intent, it's probably legit collateral — downgrade it. ("You changed `Database.query`, but it's called directly by `RedirectService` which IS in scope" → softer flag.)
   - **Local embeddings** for semantic similarity so "throttle" matches "rate limit", "auth" matches "login". Small model, still no network at runtime.
   - **History-learned pairs:** symbols that always change together in this repo's git log aren't scope creep.

2. **Adaptive depth.** Fixed `--depth 2` misses deep ripples on a signature change. If `dependents_count > 15`, walk to depth 3–4 for that symbol only.

3. **Real coverage, not just selection.** Today "covers X" = *a test reaches X in the graph*. Cross-reference an `lcov`/coverage report if the repo produces one, and flag `signature_changed` symbols where **no test asserts the new shape**.

4. **Service-boundary awareness.** Map paths → services (from `package.json` workspaces / `go.mod` / a config file) and say *"this change crosses from `redirect-svc` into `shorten-svc`"* — the scariest kind of blast radius.

5. **Trend baseline.** "This repo's PRs touch ~7 nodes on average; this one touches 19" — anomaly signal, not just absolute numbers.

6. **Suppression.** `.blastradiusignore` or a `scope-ok` PR label so an intentional wide refactor doesn't nag on every push.

## Ambitious (the "where this goes" slide)

- **MCP / agent tool.** Wrap `review()` as an MCP server so a coding agent calls `blast_radius(base, head)` *before* it edits — "here's what you're about to affect, and the 6 tests to run after." This is the brief's "workflow for agents" taken literally. The core use-case is already pure and adapter-free, so it's a new entry point beside `cli.ts`, nothing else changes.
- **Checkpoint-native intent.** Replace the `.entire/intent/<id>.json` file read with a real `entire checkpoint show` / `entire search` call — the actual captured session, and the full "did the agent do what it was asked" loop.
- **Pre-merge gate with policy.** `fail-on-findings` exists; add policy tiers ("block if a `breaking` change has an untested caller").

## What to say to a judge who asks "what's next"

> *"Three directions. Make the scope heuristic graph-aware — a change close to an in-scope symbol is probably fine. Turn warnings into actions — list the exact call sites to fix. And expose it as an MCP tool so agents run it before editing, not just humans after."*

## How to read those two sections

### Recommended tests — 4, covers every changed symbol

> `npx vitest run test/database.test.ts test/rate-limit.test.ts test/redirect.test.ts test/link-repo.test.ts`

**"Instead of running all 13 test files, run these 4 — they're the ones that actually touch your change."** Copy the command, paste it, done.

**"Why these tests"** table — one row per selected test:

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| **Test** | the test file, clickable to the source |
| **Covers** | which changed symbols this test reaches through the call graph. `link-repo.test.ts` reaches 7 things because it calls `LinkRepo` methods which call `Database.query` — so running it exercises the whole chain you touched |
| **Distance** | graph hops from the test to the nearest changed symbol. `1` = the test calls the changed code directly (strongest signal). A `3` would be "reaches it eventually" |

"covers every changed symbol" = every function/method you modified has at least one test in this list. If it said "covers all but 2", those 2 would be listed as **gaps** — change them and verify by hand.

### Full blast radius — 19 nodes across 11 files

> CALLED_BY: 8 · FILE_CHANGES_WITH: 4 · RETURNS_TYPE: 3 · CALLS: 2 · SIBLING: 1 · PARAM_TYPE: 1

The 19 affected nodes, **bucketed by relationship**:
- **CALLED_BY: 8** — 8 symbols call your changed code (the ripple upward)
- **FILE_CHANGES_WITH: 4** — 4 files that historically change alongside yours (git-history signal)
- **RETURNS_TYPE: 3 / PARAM_TYPE: 1** — 4 places use a type your change touches
- **CALLS: 2** — 2 things your changed code now calls
- **SIBLING: 1** — 1 method in the same class

`8 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 19`. It's a one-line profile of *how* the change spreads, not just *how much*.

## "Full node list is in the JSON / SARIF output (--format json)"

The markdown comment shows the **summary** (counts + the important findings) to keep the PR comment short. The **complete list of all 19 nodes** — every name, file, line, distance, relation — is in the machine formats:

```bash
blast-radius review --base main --head HEAD --format json    # the whole AnalysisReport object
blast-radius review --base main --head HEAD --format sarif    # findings as SARIF → GitHub "Code scanning" tab
```

The Action already produces both (SARIF goes to the Security tab, JSON is for agents/scripts). The markdown just doesn't dump all 19 rows inline because it'd bury the 4 findings that matter.

**Honestly** — I could put the full 19-row list in a collapsed `<details>` in the comment too. Right now it's a deliberate omission, not a limitation.

## Making it more visually appealing

GitHub PR comments allow more than we're using. Options, biggest impact first:

1. **A Mermaid graph diagram** — GitHub renders ```mermaid blocks inline. Show the changed symbol at the center with arrows out to its blast radius, findings in red. This literally *shows the graph* — huge for a "Graph Intelligence" track demo. ~1 hr.
2. **A scoreboard header with shield badges** — `![](https://img.shields.io/badge/nodes-19-blue)` style row instead of the plain text line. Crisper, scannable. ~20 min.
3. **Severity as colored bars / a mini bar chart** in unicode block chars for the relation breakdown. ~20 min.
4. **Full 19-node list** in a collapsed section with a clean table. ~15 min.
5. **Job summary** can take even richer HTML than the comment — could make that version fancier.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text:
Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose - where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on - the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves - and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes - the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on - no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` - no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end - never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11-13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool - simplify instead.

Technical documentation

How Blast Radius works behind the scenes

Blast Radius reads a pull request, asks Entire Graph what the change touches, checks that against what the change was supposed to do, and picks the tests that actually cover it. This document explains every step — in plain English first, then in full technical depth, with a complete worked example.

Track 02 · Build with Graph Intelligence github.com/entire-hackathon/blast-radius

00What it is, in one minute

A pull request shows you a diff. A diff does not show you the consequences of that diff.

If you change one line in a function that thirty other functions call, the diff still shows one line. The reviewer approves it without seeing the thirty. CI then runs the entire test suite because nothing told it which tests are relevant. And nobody notices that the change — meant to be small — quietly grew a second, unrelated modification.

Blast Radius fixes all three on every PR, and posts a single comment:

  • The blast radius — every function, type, and file the change reaches through the dependency graph, not just the ones in the diff.
  • Scope drift — changed code that shares no vocabulary with the stated intent of the PR, and that other code depends on. Flagged, with the graph path as proof.
  • A minimal test set — the specific tests that exercise the change, ranked by how close they are in the graph, with a copy-paste command. "Run these six, not all eighty."

Every claim in the comment links to the exact path through the graph that justifies it, so a reviewer verifies rather than trusts.

Key idea The graph is used as a dependency, not a display. Raw graph output is never shown on its own — it is joined, scored, and turned into a decision (approve / look here / run these). That is the point of the "Graph Intelligence" track.

01The stack — what is written in what, and why

Blast Radius itself

Concern Choice Why this one
Language TypeScript, ESM, Node ≥ 20 One language for the CLI and the GitHub Action. Static types across the whole pipeline.
Test runner vitest TypeScript-native, fast, snapshot support. 72 tests, run in ~3 s.
Schema validation zod Every blob of external JSON (graph output, GitHub API) is parsed through a schema on entry. The domain only ever sees validated objects.
CLI parsing commander Standard, minimal, no magic.
Subprocess execa Runs entire-graph, git, gh with an argv array — never a shell string, so a ref or symbol name can't inject.
Lint boundary eslint-plugin-boundaries Enforces the hexagonal import rule (§3) at CI time — the architecture can't rot.
Build tsc → dist/ No bundler. bin points at dist/cli.js.
Delivery Composite GitHub Action (action.yml) Shell steps, no bundled JS action, no dist/ webpack step to debug.

~3,300 lines of TypeScript across 37 source files · 72 tests · MIT

Entire Graph — the engine underneath

Blast Radius does not parse code or build a graph itself. It shells out to entire-graph, a separate binary:

  • Written in Go, with cgo bindings to tree-sitter (real language grammars in C, not regex).
  • No-egress — no network calls, no model calls, no API keys. The analysis is fully local and deterministic: same repo + same commit ⇒ same graph.
  • Parses 36 languages semantically (Go, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C++, Rust, Ruby…) and ~150 more for file inventory.
Division of labour entire-graph answers "what calls this / what does this touch." Blast Radius decides "so what" — it joins those answers across every changed symbol, compares them to the intent, ranks the tests, and writes the comment.

02Repository layout — every file, what it does

blast-radius/
src/domain/            pure logic — no file, network, or process I/O
  model.ts           value objects + the AnalysisReport output schema (zod)
  graph-schema.ts    lenient zod schemas for raw entire-graph JSON
  graph-mapping.ts   raw JSON → domain value objects (pure mappers)
  errors.ts          BlastRadiusError + a Result<T,E> railway type
  pipeline.ts        chain() / fanOut() combinators
  blast-radius.ts    the fold: union + dedupe the per-symbol impact lists
  summary.ts         counts by module / service / relation
  test-detect.ts     is this symbol a test? (configurable globs)
  test-selection.ts  proximity ranking, minimal cover, run-command synthesis
  intent-keywords.ts tokeniser, stemmer, lexical overlap
  intent.ts          build an IntentModel from raw text
  report.ts          assemble + validate the AnalysisReport
  scope-creep/       the scope-drift strategies (Strategy pattern)
    strategy.ts        ScopeCreepStrategy interface + CompositeStrategy
    keyword-overlap.ts unrelated change with dependents → finding
    dependents.ts      wide-reaching change → finding

src/ports/             interfaces only — the seams
  graph-provider.ts  diff() + impact()
  intent-source.ts   get(prContext)
  report-sink.ts     publish(rendered)
  renderer.ts        render(report)

src/adapters/          implementations of the ports
  graph/entire-graph-cli.ts  runs the real binary (execa)
  graph/fixture.ts           reads recorded JSON — dev, tests, offline
  intent/pr-body.ts          PR title + description
  intent/github-issue.ts     gh issue view for a linked issue
  intent/checkpoint-trailer.ts Entire-Checkpoint git trailer + .entire/intent/<id>.json
  intent/composite.ts        try each source in order; first wins
  sink/stdout.ts · file.ts · github-comment.ts  github-comment upserts one comment
  render/markdown.ts · json.ts · sarif.ts

src/app/
  review.ts          the use-case — the pipeline, spelled out
  config.ts          zod config schema, flag + env merge
  github-context.ts  reads GITHUB_EVENT_PATH / env in a runner

src/composition-root.ts  the ONLY file that imports adapters/ — wires everything
src/cli.ts              commander → composition root → review()

action.yml              composite GitHub Action
fixtures/               real entire-graph JSON captured from the demo repo

03Architecture — hexagonal, and why it matters here

The design is ports and adapters (hexagonal). The core logic knows nothing about GitHub, the filesystem, or the entire-graph binary. It depends only on interfaces. Every external system is an adapter behind one of those interfaces.

Why this shape, for this project

The hackathon has a "Noon Curve Ball" — a surprise constraint dropped mid-event. Hexagonal design means almost any plausible constraint is one adapter or one strategy, never a rewrite:

If the constraint is…The change is…
"support GitLab / Bitbucket"new ReportSink + IntentSource adapter
"output JUnit / a custom format"new Renderer adapter
"intent from Jira / Linear"new IntentSource; the composite already sequences them
"run as an MCP tool for agents"review() is already a pure use-case — add an entry point beside cli.ts
"change how scope drift is judged"new ScopeCreepStrategy; the pipeline doesn't change
"must work fully offline"already does — FixtureGraphAdapter + FileSink

04The Entire Graph engine — nodes, edges, commands

What it builds

entire-graph parses every file with tree-sitter and produces a typed graph of the repository:

  • Nodes — symbols: functions, methods, classes, interfaces, types, fields. Each carries a stable id, a qualified name, file:line, language, and kind.
  • Edges — about 30 typed relations between symbols, each tagged with a resolution confidence.
EdgeMeaningUsed for
CALLSA calls B — resolved from the actual call site in the ASTcallers & callees
USES_TYPE / PARAM_TYPE / RETURNS_TYPEA references type B in its body / parameters / returntype consumers
DATA_FLOWSa value flows from A to B (parameter forwarding, return threading)data-flow radius
FILE_CHANGES_WITHA's file and B's file historically change in the same commitsco-change radius
CONTAINSclass A contains method Bsiblings
HANDLES_ROUTEA is the handler for an HTTP routeservice-boundary detection

The four commands Blast Radius calls

1 · what changed
entire-graph diff --base <A> --head <B> --json
→ per-symbol change list, each with type (added|removed|renamed|
  signature_changed|body_changed) and a heuristic dependents_count

2 · what one symbol touches
entire-graph impact --symbol "Database.query" --file src/db/database.ts \
                     --depth 2 --format json
→ a bounded outward traversal, pre-sectioned:
    callers · callees · type_consumers · data_flows · co_changes · siblings

3 · distance refinement
entire-graph neighbors --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in

4 · the change's origin
# the Entire-Checkpoint: <id> trailer on the commit links it to the
# session that produced it — see §6

What one impact result actually looks like

real output · Database.query · demo repo
{
  "query": "Database.query",
  "focus": { "qualified_name": "Database.query",
             "file_path": "src/db/database.ts", "start_line": 12 },
  "callers": { "total": 5, "entries": [
    { "endpoint": { "qualified_name": "LinkRepo.byId",
                    "file_path": "src/repo/link-repo.ts", "start_line": 16 },
      "relation": "CALLS", "direction": "in", "depth": 1 },
    { "endpoint": { "qualified_name": "RedirectService.resolve" },
      "relation": "CALLS", "direction": "in", "depth": 2,
      "via": "LinkRepo.byId" },
    ... ] },
  "type_consumers": { "total": 4, "entries": [
    { "endpoint": { "qualified_name": "QueryOptions" },
      "relation": "PARAM_TYPE", "direction": "out", "depth": 1 }, ... ] },
  "stats": { "symbols": 40, "relations": 120, "completeness_level": "..." }
}
The graph does the walk Blast Radius never traverses edges itself. It calls impact once per changed symbol and gets the neighbourhood back, already sectioned and depth-tagged.

05How the blast radius is computed — the seven stages

src/app/review.ts is the whole pipeline, written out. Seven stages: three do I/O through a port, four are pure.

Stage 1 — collectChangeSet

Call diff. Validate the JSON against a zod schema. Map each row to a ChangedSymbol. Drop the noise: module-scope rows, and freshly-added fields/variables (they are just members of a new class and clutter everything downstream). 

ChangeSet {
  base, head, checkpoint?           // checkpoint id, if the diff resolved one
  symbols: ChangedSymbol[]          // { ref, changeType, dependentsCount, old/newSignature }
  changedFiles: string[]
}

Stage 2 — computeBlastRadius: this is the core

For every changed symbol, call impact. That gives N neighbourhood results that overlap — the same downstream function is often reached from two different changes. The fold merges them into one deduplicated set.

Each impact entry becomes a RadiusNode, tagged with which changed symbol it came from:

RadiusNode {
  ref            // { qualifiedName, file, line, kind, external }
  section        // callers | callees | type_consumers | data_flows | co_changes | siblings
  relation       // CALLS | CALLED_BY | USES_TYPE | DATA_FLOWS | ...
  distance       // graph hops from the nearest changed symbol (1 = direct)
  viaChain       // [ "LinkRepo.byId" ]  — the intermediate hop(s)
  originSymbols  // [ "Database.query" ] — which change(s) this derives from
  isTest         // matched against test-file globs
}

Then the fold, exactly as the code runs it:

the fold, in pseudocode
byKey = {}                              // Map<"file::name", RadiusNode>
originNames = { qualifiedName of every changed symbol }
addedNames  = { changed symbols whose type == "added" }

for node in every impact result:
    if node.external and node.section == "callees":      continue   // noise
    if node.section == "siblings"
       and every origin is in addedNames:                continue   // new-class members
    if node.qualifiedName in originNames:
        if node.section == "callers":
            record originEdge(node → its origin)                    // for the diagram
        continue                                                    // it's the blast source, not the blast
    key = node.file + "::" + node.qualifiedName
    byKey[key] = byKey.has(key) ? merge(byKey[key], node) : node

merge(a, b):  keep min(distance), union(originSymbols),
              keep whichever viaChain / callSite is non-empty,
              isTest = a.isTest or b.isTest

nodes = sort(byKey.values, by distance asc, then name)
sectionTotals[section] = count of nodes in that section

Stages 4–6 — intent, fan-out, report

Stage 4 resolves the intent (§6). Stage 5 runs three pure computations over the same blast radius — scope check (§7), test selection (§8), and a summary (counts by module / service / relation). Stage 6 assembles an AnalysisReport and validates it against its published schema before it leaves the builder — so a renderer never has to defend against a malformed report.

Stage 7 — render & publish

One or more Renderers (markdown / JSON / SARIF) turn the report into text; each goes to a ReportSink (a PR comment, a file, stdout). A failing sink is collected, not fatal — if the PR-comment sink is blocked by repository permissions, the report still lands in the job summary.

06Resolving intent — three tiers, tried in order

"Scope drift" only means something relative to what the change was meant to do. CompositeIntentSource asks three adapters in priority order and uses the first that answers.

#SourceWhere the text comes fromSetup
1 checkpoint-trailer An Entire-Checkpoint: <id> trailer on the commit (added automatically by Entire's git hooks) → the captured agent prompt. In the demo, staged as .entire/intent/<id>.json because there is no full Entire backend in the sandbox. automatic, when the team uses Entire
2 github-issue Closes #42 in the PR body → gh issue view 42 → title + body none — works on any GitHub repo
3 pr-body the PR title + description the author typed none — the universal fallback

Whichever answers, the raw text is turned into an IntentModel: a title, a body, and a set of keywords — significant terms, lowercased, stop-worded, lightly stemmed, with backtick-quoted code spans weighted in.

Production vs demo A real user never writes an intent file. Tier 2/3 need only a normal PR description. Tier 1 is a byproduct of using Entire — productionising it is swapping the .entire/intent/<id>.json read for an entire checkpoint show call.

07Scope-creep detection — the unique logic

The graph says what changed. The intent says what was asked. This is where they are compared.

Detection is a set of interchangeable strategies (Strategy pattern). Two ship; CompositeStrategy runs both and merges their findings by symbol, keeping the higher severity and unioning the evidence.

Strategy A — keyword overlap

Deliberately lexical, not embeddings — because it has to be explainable to a reviewer in one sentence: "this symbol shares no words with the ticket."

  1. nameTokens(S) = split the changed symbol's qualified name and its file path on camelCase / snake_case / / / ., lowercase, drop layout-only segments (src, internal, …) and stopwords, light-stem.
  2. overlap = |nameTokens(S) ∩ intent.keywords| / |nameTokens(S)|
  3. Emit a finding when overlap < 0.15 and S.dependentsCount ≥ 3 and the change is not a brand-new symbol.

Strategy B — dependents threshold

Any changed symbol with dependentsCount ≥ 8 is flagged as "wide-reaching," intent or no intent. A signature change here says "run tests first." On its own it is not proof of drift — combined with a keyword-overlap miss it is a strong signal.

Worked example

intent   = "Rate-limit the redirect endpoint"
keywords = { rate, limit, redirect, endpoint }

changed symbol         nameTokens                overlap   deps   →
Database.query          { database, query }        0.00      6     FLAG (medium)
LinkRepo.byId           { link, repo, id }         0.00      3     FLAG (low)
RedirectController.handle { redirect, controller,
                           handle }                0.33      2     ok — matches "redirect"
TokenBucketRateLimiter.take { token, bucket, rate,
                             limit, take }         0.60      2     ok — matches the ask

The PR said "rate-limit the redirect endpoint." It also widened Database.query and threaded the new argument through LinkRepo. Those four tokens (database, query, link, repo) appear nowhere in the intent, and six things depend on Database.query. Flagged — correctly.

08Test selection — "run these, not everything"

  1. Every node in the blast radius whose file matches a test glob (*.test.ts, *_test.go, test_*.py, **/tests/** …) is a candidate.
  2. score = 1 / (1 + distance) + (direct caller ? 0.5 : 0) — closer tests rank higher.
  3. Minimal sufficient set — greedily add candidates by score until every changed callable is covered by at least one selected test.
  4. Any changed function/method that no test reaches is reported as an explicit coverage gap — never hidden.
  5. Synthesise the run command for the detected framework:
    go test -run '^(TestA|TestB)$' ./pkg/... · npx vitest run <files> · pytest <file>::<name>
What "covers" means A selected test reaches the changed symbol through the call graph. That is test selection, not coverage measurement — it does not verify the test asserts on the new behaviour. Cross-referencing an actual coverage report is on the roadmap.

09The report & its schema

Everything above lands in one immutable AnalysisReport, versioned (schemaVersion 1.1.0) and validated on build. It is the single object every renderer consumes and the JSON output emits. 

AnalysisReport {
  schemaVersion, generatedAt
  range          { base, head, checkpoint? }
  intent         IntentModel | null
  changeSummary  { symbolCount, fileCount, widestDependents }
  changedSymbols [ { ref, changeType, dependentsCount, isFinding } ]
  radiusSummary  { totalNodes, fileCount, moduleCount, serviceCount,
                   testCount, byRelation }
  radiusNodes    [ RadiusNode ]        // the complete list, not just counts
  originEdges    [ { from, to } ]      // call edges among the changes (for the diagram)
  findings       [ { symbol, severity, strategy, reason,
                     dependentsCount, evidence[] } ]
  testPlan       { framework, selected[], command, coverageGaps[] }
}

Three renderings

  • Markdown — the PR comment: a shields.io badge strip, a Mermaid graph of the change and its callers (findings in red), the scope table, the test command, then collapsed detail.
  • JSON — the whole object, for agents and scripts.
  • SARIF 2.1.0 — findings as results, uploaded to the GitHub Code scanning tab.

10Why this is a unique product

ApproachWhat it gives youWhat it misses
IDE "find usages" callers of one symbol, on demand you have to run it per symbol, mentally union the results, and it says nothing about intent or tests
CI coverage report which lines a test suite executed runs after you've already run everything; no notion of "this PR", no scope check
LLM PR reviewer prose comments, sometimes insightful non-deterministic, unverifiable, no graph — it guesses at impact from the diff text
Raw entire-graph impact the neighbourhood of one symbol one symbol at a time; raw output; no decision — the brief explicitly says this isn't enough
Blast Radius the unioned radius of the whole change, cross-checked against the stated intent, with a minimal test set — one comment, every claim traceable to a graph path static-analysis limits (§12), stated openly

Two things make it specific rather than a wrapper:

  1. The graph is a real dependency. diff, impact, neighbors and the checkpoint trailer are joined, deduplicated, scored and turned into a decision. The raw output never appears alone.
  2. Graph findings are tied to Checkpoint intent. Both are named directions in the track brief; combining them — "the graph says X changed, the checkpoint says only Y was asked, here is the delta" — is the core of the product, not a feature bolted on.

11Plug it into your repo — and what happens behind the scenes

What the user does — once

Create one file, .github/workflows/blast-radius.yml:

name: Blast Radius
on: pull_request
permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write, security-events: write }
jobs:
  blast-radius:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }        # full history — diff needs the base
      - uses: entire-hackathon/blast-radius@v0.1.0
        with: { upload-sarif: true }

Commit it. No account, no config, no intent file. From then on, the author just writes a normal PR description.

What happens when a PR opens — step by step

  1. Checkout with full history

    fetch-depth: 0 so diff can see the base commit, not just the tip.

  2. Build or restore entire-graph

    setup-go, then go build from source — or an actions/cache hit if this version was built before. ~2–4 min cold, seconds warm.

  3. Read the PR context

    The CLI reads GITHUB_EVENT_PATH for the base/head SHAs, PR number, title, body, and builds the blob-URL base so every symbol in the comment becomes a real GitHub link.

  4. entire-graph diff --base <base sha> --head <head sha> --json

    The changed symbols, each with its dependents_count. Noise rows dropped.

  5. entire-graph impact — once per changed symbol

    Each call returns that symbol's callers, callees, type consumers, data flows, co-change files and siblings, depth-tagged. The results are folded into one deduplicated blast radius (§5).

  6. Resolve intent

    git log the head commit for an Entire-Checkpoint trailer → else parse Closes #N and gh issue view → else the PR description. Turn the text into keywords.

  7. Scope check · test selection · summary

    Three pure passes over the blast radius (§7, §8). No further I/O.

  8. Render & publish

    Markdown → gh api upserts one comment (finds its own previous comment by a hidden marker and edits it). SARIF → the Code scanning tab. Both → the job summary, which needs no write permission at all.

Total wall time on a warm cache: seconds for a small PR, a minute or two for a large one. The reviewer opens the PR to a comment that already tells them where to look and what to run.

12Limitations — stated plainly

  • Static call resolution. Dynamic dispatch, reflection, DI containers and string-keyed handlers can be missed or over-approximated. entire-graph is tree-sitter-accurate for direct calls and reports completeness: degraded when it isn't sure. Blast Radius shows the graph path so the reviewer can verify.
  • Depth 2. You see direct callers plus one transitive hop — deeper is noise for a review. Adaptive depth for high-fan-out signature changes is on the roadmap.
  • Co-change edges are correlational, mined from git history, not causal.
  • dependents_count is entire-graph's number — surfaced, not independently recomputed.
  • Scope overlap is lexical. "throttle" won't match "rate limit" yet. Graph-anchored and embedding-based scoring are the planned next steps.
  • Test "coverage" is reachability, not assertion (see §8).

13Full worked example — the demo PR

Repo: linkshrink, a tiny URL shortener. Branch feat/redirect-rate-limit. Stated intent (from the checkpoint trailer): "Rate-limit the redirect endpoint."

The diff

src/service/rate-limit.ts   + TokenBucketRateLimiter       (new, in scope)
src/http/redirect-handler.ts   handleRedirect body_changed    (in scope)
src/db/types.ts             + QueryOptions              (new)
src/db/database.ts          Database.query  signature_changed  ← not in the ask
src/repo/link-repo.ts       LinkRepo.byId / .save / .hit  signature_changed  ← not in the ask

Blast radius, after the fold

The comment it posts

badges  blast radius: 19 nodes · modules: 8 · scope: 4 findings
        tests: 4 selected · intent: checkpoint-trailer

scope check — 4 outside the ask
🟠  Database.query   src/db/database.ts:12   no vocabulary overlap · 6 deps
🟡  LinkRepo.byId    src/repo/link-repo.ts:16   no vocabulary overlap · 3 deps
🟡  LinkRepo.save    …                          · 3 deps
🟡  LinkRepo.hit     …                          · 3 deps

evidence · Database.query
- intent (checkpoint-trailer): "Rate-limit the redirect endpoint"
- changed here — signature changed, 6 dependents — src/db/database.ts:12
- reaches LinkRepo.byId → RedirectService.resolve

recommended tests — 4, covers every changed symbol
npx vitest run test/database.test.ts test/rate-limit.test.ts \
               test/redirect.test.ts test/link-repo.test.ts

full blast radius — 19 nodes
CALLED_BY 8 · SIBLING 4 · FILE_CHANGES_WITH 4 · RETURNS_TYPE 3 · CALLS 2 · PARAM_TYPE 1

The reviewer reads: the redirect handler change is fine, but the PR also re-plumbed the entire data-access layer — four changes, none named in the ticket — and here are the four tests that cover it. Every line links to the code.

See it live on the demo PR →

A 14-section technical reference, sticky-sidebar navigation, same visual identity as the pitch deck (dark-first, monospace-forward, ember accent). Every diagram is hand-drawn inline SVG, theme-aware.

## What's in it

## Diagrams (5, all inline SVG)

architecture layers · the 7-stage pipeline · the fold flowchart · the scope-creep decision flow · the plug-in sequence diagram · the worked-example blast rings

Open it and skim. If any diagram clips or text is unreadable on your screen, tell me which section and I'll fix it once.
here what does the color coding means?

That's the Mermaid graph from the live PR comment. Five colors, and the arrows matter too.

## The nodes

| Color | Class | Means |
|---|---|---|
| 🔴 **red/pink** | `finding` | Changed **and flagged** — outside the stated intent. `Database.query`, `LinkRepo.byId`, `LinkRepo.hit`, `LinkRepo.save` |
| 🟡 **amber/yellow** | `changed` | Changed but **in scope** — matches the intent or is new code. `handleRedirect`, `TokenBucketRateLimiter.take` |
| ⬜ **grey** | `caller` | **Not changed** — it just calls into the changed code, so it's in the blast radius. `route`, `ShortenService.create` |
| 🟢 **green** | `test` | A **test** that reaches the change through the graph. `redirect.test.ts` |
| (grey, only if truncated) | `more` | "+N more callers" when the diagram hits its node cap |

## The arrows

`A → B` means **A depends on / calls B**. Read them from the outside in:

- `LinkRepo.byId → Database.query` — byId calls query
- `handleRedirect → LinkRepo.byId / .hit / TokenBucketRateLimiter.take` — the redirect handler reaches all of those
- `route → handleRedirect`, `redirect.test.ts → handleRedirect` — what sits upstream of the handler

## The story it tells at a glance

The **amber** redirect-handler change (intended) is fine. But it dragged in the **red** `LinkRepo` methods, which all funnel into the **red** `Database.query` — a data-layer re-plumbing nobody asked for. The **green** `redirect.test.ts` is one of the tests that covers it.

## Gap I should close

The comment doesn't include a legend, so the colors are only obvious if you already know the scheme. **Want me to add a one-line legend right under the diagram?** Something like:

> `🔴 flagged · 🟡 changed, in scope · ⬜ caller · 🟢 test`

Quick change to the markdown renderer, tests stay green.

Legend is live. CI green (`9a6be28`).

The [PR #1 comment](https://github.com/entire-hackathon/blast-radius-demo/pull/1) now has this line right under the graph:

> 🔴 flagged — outside the stated intent · 🟡 changed, in scope · ⬜ caller (unchanged, in the radius) · 🟢 covering test · arrow = calls / depends on

Only the categories actually present in a given diagram show up in its legend — so a clean PR with no findings won't display the 🔴 entry.
And what are these colors?

These are **severity** dots — a different scale from the diagram colors. Here they rank *how alarming each finding is*, driven by the dependent count.

| Dot | Severity | Rule | In your screenshot |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔴 | high | ≥ 15 dependents | — |
| 🟠 | medium | ≥ 6 dependents | `Database.query` (6) |
| 🟡 | low | < 6 dependents | `LinkRepo.byId / .save / .hit` (3 each) |

So all four are flagged for the same reason (*"no vocabulary overlap with the stated intent"*), but `Database.query` gets an orange dot because **6 things depend on it** — changing it is riskier than changing the `LinkRepo` methods that 3 things depend on.

The number in the **Dependents** column is exactly what drives the dot. It comes straight from `entire-graph diff` (its `dependents_count`).

### Two different color schemes — worth keeping straight

| Where | What the color means |
|---|---|
| **Scope-check table** (this screenshot) | 🔴🟠🟡 = severity of the finding, by dependent count |
| **Mermaid diagram** (earlier screenshot) | 🔴 flagged / 🟡 changed-in-scope / ⬜ caller / 🟢 test — node *category*, not severity |

The overlap (both use red/yellow) is a little unfortunate. If it's confusing in the demo, I can switch the diagram's "changed, in scope" from yellow to blue so the two schemes don't collide. Say the word.

what is this color? ⬜ caller (unchanged, in the radius) ·

The **pale grey box** in the diagram — `#eef2f6` fill, grey border. In your earlier diagram screenshot, `route` and `ShortenService.create` were these.

The legend uses `⬜` (white square) because there's no grey-square emoji that renders reliably everywhere — it stands in for that pale grey node.

**What a "caller" node is:** a function that *calls into* the changed code but **was not itself changed**. It's in the blast radius (a change to `Database.query` could affect it), but there's nothing for the reviewer to flag about it — it's just showing you the reach.

Contrast the four node types in the diagram:

| Box | Was it changed? | Reviewer action |
|---|---|---|
| 🟥 red | yes, and flagged | look at this — it's outside the ask |
| 🟨 yellow | yes, in scope | expected, part of the intended change |
| ⬜ grey | **no** — it just calls the changed code | context only — shows what's downstream |
| 🟩 green | no — it's a test | run it |
here what is depicting ⬜ grey	no — it just calls the changed code	context only — shows what's downstream

I got the direction wrong earlier — let me correct it. The grey nodes are **upstream**, not downstream.

## Reading this diagram

Arrows mean **"calls"**. Follow them left to right:

- `route` **→** `handleRedirect` — the router calls the redirect handler
- `ShortenService.create` **→** `LinkRepo.save` — the shorten service calls `LinkRepo.save`
- `LinkRepo.save` **→** `Database.query` — and that calls the database

## What the two grey nodes are telling you

**`route`** and **`ShortenService.create`** are code that **calls something the PR changed, but wasn't changed itself.**

- `ShortenService.create` calls `LinkRepo.save`. The PR changed `LinkRepo.save`'s signature (🟥). So `ShortenService.create` **might now be broken or need updating** — even though it's not in the diff. That's the blast radius: the change *reaches* it.
- `route` calls `handleRedirect`, which the PR changed (🟨). Same idea — `route` sits on the affected path.

So it's not "context only" — I undersold it. Grey nodes are **the callers that inherit the risk**: places a reviewer should check still compile and behave correctly after this change, despite not appearing in the diff.

## The corrected table

| Box | Changed in this PR? | Why it's in the diagram |
|---|---|---|
| 🟥 red | yes — **flagged** | changed, and outside the stated intent |
| 🟨 yellow | yes — in scope | the intended change |
| ⬜ grey | **no** | it *calls* changed code, so the change reaches it — check it didn't break |
| 🟩 green | no — it's a test | it exercises the changed code — run it |

Two views of the same analysis. **Badges = the counts. Graph = the shape.**

## The badges — a one-line scorecard

| Badge | Means | Where it's computed |
|---|---|---|
| `blast radius · 19 nodes` | the change reaches **19 distinct symbols/files** once you follow the graph (callers + callees + types + data-flow + co-change + siblings, deduplicated) | the fold, §5 |
| `modules · 8` | those 19 nodes span **8 top-level folders** | summary |
| `scope · 4 findings` | **4 changed symbols** look outside the stated intent | scope check, §7 |
| `tests · 4 selected` | **4 test files** cover the change | test selection, §8 |
| `intent · checkpoint-trailer` | the intent came from the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer (shown on the line right below) | intent resolution, §6 |

## The graph — a curated slice of those 19 nodes

The diagram is **not** all 19. It's the **call skeleton around the change** — changed symbols plus their direct callers and any test that reaches them, capped at 16 nodes so it stays readable. The full 19 are in the "Full blast radius" table further down the comment.

Nodes in this graph: 4 red + 2 amber + 2 grey + 1 green = **9 of the 19**.

## How they line up

| Badge says | In the graph you see |
|---|---|
| `scope · 4 findings` | exactly the **4 🟥 red boxes** — `Database.query`, `LinkRepo.byId`, `.hit`, `.save` |
| `intent · checkpoint-trailer` = *"Rate-limit the redirect endpoint"* | the 🟨 amber boxes (`handleRedirect`, `TokenBucketRateLimiter.take`) match that intent; the 🟥 red ones don't |
| `tests · 4 selected` | the graph shows **1** of them (`redirect.test.ts` 🟩) — the other 3 reach the change through paths the diagram didn't draw; all 4 are in the test table |
| `blast radius · 19 nodes` | the graph draws 9; the ⬜ grey nodes (`route`, `ShortenService.create`) are examples of the "reached but not changed" set |

## What the picture tells you that the badges can't

The badges say *"4 findings."* The graph shows **why they're one problem, not four**: `LinkRepo.byId / .hit / .save` all point into `Database.query`, and `handleRedirect` (the intended change) is what pulled them in. It's a single database-layer re-plumbing that rode along with the rate-limiting work — visible only as a shape.
